text: Films show the asteroid belt as a shooting gallery you have to dodge. The real belt is mostly nothing. The asteroids in it work out to roughly 600,000 miles apart on average, more than twice the distance from Earth to the moon. Spacecraft fly straight through without steering around anything.
more: Pioneer 10 went in first, entering the belt in July 1972 and coming out the far side in February 1973 with fewer dust hits than anyone expected. Pioneer 11, both Voyagers, Galileo, Cassini, Juno and New Horizons have all crossed since. Standing on one asteroid, you would be lucky to see a second one at all.

text: The largest thing in the asteroid belt is Ceres, about 585 miles (940 km) across. Giuseppe Piazzi found it on the first night of 1801. It was the very first asteroid anyone spotted. NASA's Dawn spacecraft arrived in 2015 and went into orbit around it. That made Ceres the first dwarf planet ever visited.
more: Dawn photographed a crater called Occator with a startling bright patch in the middle. The patch is far brighter than the gray ground around it. Ceres is also counted as a dwarf planet. So it holds two titles at once. Biggest asteroid, and nearest dwarf planet to us.

text: On 24 August 2006 astronomers met in Prague and voted on what the word planet means. It goes round the sun. It is round itself. It has swept its own orbital lane clear. Pluto passes the first two and fails the third. So it was moved to a new category, dwarf planet.
more: Nothing about Pluto changed that day. The definition did. Pluto shares its region of the solar system with Eris and a crowd of other bodies of similar size. That is exactly what failing to clear your neighborhood looks like. Plenty of astronomers still call the rule a bad one.

text: New Horizons had one shot at Pluto. On 14 July 2015 it went past at around 32,000 miles an hour, 7,800 miles (12,500 km) above the surface, with less than half an hour to photograph the whole world. The pictures came back showing a pale heart and a range of mountains.
more: The heart is named Tombaugh Regio, after Clyde Tombaugh, who found Pluto in 1930. Its left half, Sputnik Planitia, is a 600-mile plain of frozen nitrogen without a single crater on it. The mountains beside it stand about 11,000 feet (3,400 m) high and are made of water ice, which at Pluto's temperature is as hard as rock.

text: The largest meteorite anyone has found is still lying exactly where it landed. Hoba, in Namibia, weighs over 60 tons and measures about 9 feet by 9 feet by 3 feet thick. A farmer's plow struck it in 1920. Nobody has ever moved it, because nobody can.
more: It is a slab of metal, roughly 84 percent iron and 16 percent nickel with a trace of cobalt. Visitors and collectors have chipped pieces off over the years, so it weighs a little less now than when it was found. It sits in an open stone amphitheatre and you can walk up and put your hand flat on it.

text: On 15 February 2013 a rock about 60 feet (18 m) across came in over Chelyabinsk in Russia and blew apart roughly 18 miles up. Nothing hit the city; the shock wave did. It blew in windows across a wide strip of ground and cut about 1,500 people with flying glass.
more: Nobody was killed. The airburst released energy on the order of 400 to 600 kilotons of TNT. That makes it the largest such event over a populated place in living memory. Russian drivers commonly run dashboard cameras. The whole thing was filmed from dozens of angles at once, and can be watched frame by frame.

text: Edmond Halley noticed in 1705 that bright comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 all followed the same path, and said it was one comet coming back. He predicted the next return for 1758. It arrived, sixteen years after he died. Chinese astronomers had logged the same comet as far back as 240 BC.
more: It came again in 1835, 1910 and 1986. It is due on 28 July 2061. The 1066 visit is stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry, with a row of men pointing up at it. In 1986 the European probe Giotto flew close enough to photograph the solid lump at the center. It turned out to be a very dark peanut-shaped thing about nine miles long.

text: OSIRIS-REx flew to the asteroid Bennu, touched it for a few seconds, grabbed a handful and came home. The capsule landed in the Utah desert on 24 September 2023 with 4.29 ounces (121.6 g) of Bennu inside. People can now hold pieces of an asteroid in a laboratory.
more: The collecting arm scooped up so much material that a flap jammed open. Grains began drifting away into space. The team stowed the sample early rather than lose more. The mission needed 60 grams to count as a success. It came back with twice that.

text: Japan brought asteroid samples home before NASA's OSIRIS-REx did. Hayabusa2 spent about eighteen months at the asteroid Ryugu. It fired a copper slug into the asteroid to expose material from below the surface. It dropped a capsule into the South Australian desert on 6 December 2020. Inside were 5.4 grams of Ryugu, roughly a teaspoon.
more: A helicopter crew tracked the capsule down by its radio beacon. They found it sitting intact in the sand at Woomera. Nobody had ever collected material from beneath an asteroid's surface before, as well as from the top. That matters, because the top has been sitting out in the open.

text: A shooting star is usually a grain of sand. Most meteors come from specks smaller than a grain of rice, moving fast enough that the air ahead of them glows white. They burn out 50 to 75 miles (80 to 120 km) up, far above any aircraft, and the streak lasts under a second.
more: The three words are worth keeping straight. The pebble out in space is a meteoroid. The streak of light is the meteor. A piece that survives and reaches the ground is a meteorite. Most meteorites in the world's collections were picked up in Antarctica. Dark rocks show plainly on blue ice, and the ice flow piles them up in a few spots. Over 35,000 have been recovered there.

text: The Perseids arrive the same week every August because Earth crosses the same trail of comet dust every year. The comet that left it is 109P/Swift-Tuttle. The peak is the night of 12 to 13 August, and at a properly dark site with no moon people count 50 to 100 an hour.
tryit: Mark 12 August on the calendar. Get away from streetlights, look up and away from the moon, and start watching around 11 pm. The rate climbs through the night and is best in the couple of hours before dawn.

text: A comet's tail does not trail behind it like smoke off a train. It points away from the sun, always. Sunlight and the stream of particles blowing off the sun push the dust and gas straight outward. So a comet on its way back out of the solar system travels tail first.
more: There are usually two tails, and they point slightly differently. The gas tail glows bluish and runs almost exactly away from the sun. The dust tail is broader, whiter and curved, because the dust grains keep some of the comet's own motion as they drift.

text: On 12 November 2014 a lander called Philae was dropped onto comet 67P. Its harpoons failed to fire. It bounced, drifted for nearly two hours in the comet's almost non-existent gravity, and came down again about half a mile away in shadow. It still worked for around 64 hours.
more: It was the first landing on a comet, ever. The mother ship Rosetta had taken ten years to get there. Because Philae ended up out of the sunlight, its solar panels could not keep the batteries up, but it sent its measurements home before it went quiet.

text: Genesis 1:14 says the lights in the sky were set there "for signs and for seasons, and for days and years". The small stuff keeps that kind of time too. Edmond Halley predicted his comet's return decades ahead, and it arrived. The Perseids turn up in the same week of every single August.
more: This is what made Halley's prediction so convincing to people at the time. He was not describing a wonder; he was setting a date, publicly, for something nobody alive would check for 53 years. Then it turned up.

text: The color of a star is a thermometer reading. Split its light into a spectrum and you can measure how hot the surface is. Betelgeuse, the orange star on Orion's shoulder, comes out near 3,500 K. Rigel, the blue-white one at his foot, is around 12,000 K. Red is cool, blue is hot.
more: This is not guesswork about what a star is made of or what it is doing. Put a poker in a fire and it goes dull red, then orange, then white as it heats. Same physics, pointed at a light source and read off with an instrument.
tryit: On a winter evening find Orion. Look at the star at the top left of the four corners, then the one at the bottom right, and go back and forth a few times. Betelgeuse is clearly orange. Rigel is white with a blue edge. You are seeing a temperature difference with bare eyes.

text: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, magnitude minus 1.46, and it is bright for two reasons at once. It genuinely puts out more light than the sun, and it is close, 8.6 light-years off, one of our nearest neighbors. Brightness in the sky always mixes those two things together.
more: Sirius has a companion, Sirius B, which is about ten thousand times fainter and only turns up in a good telescope. The two swing around each other once every fifty years, and that orbit has been tracked, drawn and timed by people at the eyepiece. In winter, follow the three stars of Orion's belt down and to the left and they point straight at Sirius.

text: Hold a finger up and close one eye, then the other. The finger jumps against the far wall. That jump is parallax, and it is how the distance to nearby stars is measured. Earth's two eyes are its position in January and its position in July, and it is the star that does the jumping.
more: The angle involved is tiny, but once you have measured it, plain geometry gives you the distance. Nothing has to be assumed about the star itself. Of all the ways of getting a distance in astronomy, this is the only one that is pure measurement.
tryit: Hold your thumb at arm's length and blink one eye, then the other. Now bring it in to a foot away and try again. The nearer it is, the further it jumps. That is exactly the relationship astronomers use, just with a much longer gap between the two eyes.

text: Friedrich Bessel was the first person to measure the distance to a star. In 1838 he published a measured parallax for the star 61 Cygni: 0.314 of an arcsecond, roughly the width of a coin seen from ten miles away. That put 61 Cygni about 10 light-years off. The modern figure is 11.4, so he was close.
more: Bessel was not alone for long. Struve and Henderson published parallaxes for Vega and Alpha Centauri within about a year of him. John Herschel called Bessel's result "the greatest and most glorious triumph which practical astronomy has ever witnessed". Before 1838 nobody had a measured distance to any star at all.

text: The nearest star to the sun is Proxima Centauri, 4.24 light-years away, and you cannot see it. It is far too faint for the naked eye, around magnitude 11. Robert Innes found it in 1915 by comparing photographs of the same patch taken years apart and spotting one dot that had shifted.
more: Its distance is known by parallax, the measuring trick Friedrich Bessel first used on a star in 1838. It was measured independently by Joan Voute in 1917 and Harold Alden in 1928. The nearest star to us is invisible without a telescope, and the brightest star in the sky is not the nearest one. There is no rule that says close means bright.

text: Orion is not a group of stars. It is a group of directions. The three belt stars look evenly spaced in a neat row, but they are nothing like neighbors: Alnitak is put at around 1,260 light-years and Alnilam at nearly 2,000. Move far enough sideways and the hunter falls apart.
more: Those two distances are worked out rather than measured with geometry. They come from comparing how bright each star looks with how bright it is taken to be. So an assumption is baked into the numbers. The point survives whatever the numbers do. A constellation is a pattern seen from one particular place. That place is here.

text: On 4 July 1054 Chinese astronomers wrote down a guest star near the southern horn of Taurus. It had not been there before. It was bright enough to see in broad daylight for 23 days, stayed visible at night for 653 days, then faded out. No European record of it survives.
more: The dates are exact because the observers logged them. First seen 4 July 1054. Last seen 17 April 1056. In that same spot there is now a faint tangle of glowing gas. Charles Messier put it at the very top of his catalog as M1. Everyone calls it the Crab Nebula.

text: Ian Shelton was working at an observatory in Chile on 23 February 1987. He developed a photographic plate and found a bright star in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It was not on any of his earlier plates. He walked outside and checked with his own eyes. It was there. It was the first supernova visible without a telescope since 1604.
more: Hours before anyone saw the light, detectors buried underground in Japan, in Ohio and in the Caucasus each caught a short burst of neutrinos. About two dozen particle hits, inside a few seconds. It is the only time that has ever happened.

text: Betelgeuse dimmed, and people noticed with their eyes. Between late 2019 and February 2020 it lost roughly two thirds of its brightness. Hubble and the big telescopes in Chile watched the whole thing. A cloud of dust thrown off the star had drifted across about a quarter of its face.
more: The Very Large Telescope in Chile photographed the star's disk going lopsided as the patch darkened. In the months before, Hubble tracked dense material moving outward through the star's atmosphere. The cloud ended up more than a hundred million miles across. Betelgeuse was back to its usual brightness by the end of 2020.

text: Stars twinkle and planets mostly do not. A star is so far off that it arrives as a single point of light, and any wobble in the air shoves that whole point sideways. A planet arrives as a tiny disc, which is many points at once, and the wobbles cancel each other out.
more: Next clear night, hunt for something bright that is not flickering. Steady light, especially low in the sky, is usually a planet. Compare it against a star at the same height above the horizon and the difference shows up in a couple of seconds.

text: The brightness scale runs backwards, and it is Hipparchus's fault. He sorted the stars into six ranks and called the brightest ones stars of the first magnitude. The system stuck, so bigger numbers now mean fainter stars. Sirius comes out at minus 1.46. The faintest an ordinary eye can catch is about 6.
more: Each step of one magnitude is a brightness ratio of about 2.5. Five steps is therefore a factor of 100. That was chosen deliberately in the 1850s. It fits the old eyeball rankings onto a proper measured scale without throwing the ancient numbers away.

text: Algol loses about two thirds of its light and gets it back, over and over, every 2 days and 21 hours. John Goodricke, a deaf teenager in York, timed the cycle and in 1783 said plainly what it meant: a second star was passing in front of the first.
more: He was 18 when he started watching. He was 19 when the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal for it. He died at 21. He was also right. Algol is a pair of stars circling each other, edge-on from where we sit. The dip you can follow with your own eyes is one crossing the other.

text: A European spacecraft called Gaia spent years repeating the parallax measurement Friedrich Bessel first managed in 1838. It measured positions and parallaxes for more than 1.8 billion stars. Look up at almost anything you can see with your eyes. Its distance is now a measured number, not an educated guess.
more: Gaia had to pin down angles smaller than a thousandth of an arcsecond. That is about the width of a human hair seen from ten miles away. It managed it by scanning the entire sky over and over. Each time round, it compared where every star appeared to sit.

text: Under a genuinely dark sky, an ordinary eye can pick out about 9,100 stars across the whole sphere. Only half of them are above you at any moment. Psalm 147:4 says of God, "he determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names." Somebody counted first.
more: The figure comes from catalogues of everything brighter than magnitude 6.5, which totals 9,096 stars over the entire sky. From one spot, with haze thickening near the horizon, most people actually see two or three thousand. Genesis 1:16 covers the lot in a single short clause: "and the stars".

text: Hanging below Orion's belt is a fuzzy patch you can see with your eyes on a clear winter night. That is the Orion Nebula, a glowing cloud of gas and dust about 1,344 light-years off. People call it a stellar nursery because they think stars form inside it. Nobody has watched one form.
more: The distance is one of very few outside the solar system that is straight geometry. Radio telescopes spread across the United States measured the parallax of stars sitting inside the nebula and got 1,344 light-years, give or take 20. What is in the cloud has been measured. What is happening in it has not.
tryit: On a winter evening find the three belt stars and look at the short line hanging below them, Orion's sword. The middle star of the sword is not a star. Through binoculars it opens out into a gray-green cloud with a knot of light in the center.

text: The Pleiades look like a tiny dipper rather than a fuzzy blob. Most people pick out six or seven stars in it. Binoculars turn that into dozens. The cluster sits about 444 light-years away. That number is measured, from the parallax of individual member stars. The Gaia spacecraft took those readings.
more: The cluster has more than a thousand stars in it. Almost every culture with a clear sky has noticed it and given it a name. It is not hard to see why: a small tight knot of blue-white stars in an otherwise empty patch of sky.
tryit: Look east on an fall evening for a small misty smudge of stars. Count how many you can separate with just your eyes. Then raise binoculars and count again. Six or seven usually becomes forty or more.

text: The Andromeda galaxy is the most distant thing a person can see without equipment. From a dark site it is a faint oval several full moons long. Its distance is put at about 2.5 million light-years, and that figure is worked out rather than measured with geometry.
more: It comes from a kind of star whose true output is taken to be tied to how fast it pulses. Compare how bright those stars look in Andromeda with how bright they are assumed to be, and the difference gives a distance. Edwin Hubble did it first in 1923 using the 100-inch telescope at Mount Wilson, and his answer then was about a third of today's.
tryit: In fall find the Great Square of Pegasus, then the two chains of stars trailing off its top left corner. Andromeda is a faint oval near the second star of the upper chain. Look slightly to one side of it and it brightens, which is a real trick and not your imagination.

text: The Milky Way looks like a band rather than a spiral because we are inside it, looking along the flat part from within. On a dark night it runs right across the sky like something spilled. It is thickest and brightest toward Sagittarius, which is the direction of the middle.
more: You are looking through more stars when you look along the disc than when you look out of it, which is the whole reason the band exists. It is not a cloud. Galileo settled that in 1610 by pointing a telescope at it and watching the glow break into separate stars. To see it you need a moonless night away from town and twenty minutes without looking at a phone; then face south in summer.

text: For a very long time nobody knew what the Milky Way was made of. In 1610 Galileo turned his small telescope on it and the glow broke apart into individual stars, each too faint to see on its own. He wrote it up in a short book, Sidereus Nuncius, published that March.
more: The same book reported mountains and craters on the moon. It also reported four points of light shuffling around Jupiter. He sketched their positions on 64 separate nights, between 7 January and 2 March 1610. Only then was he willing to publish.

text: A globular cluster is a ball of stars packed so tightly the middle looks solid. M13, in Hercules, holds somewhere between a hundred thousand and six hundred thousand stars. Halley found it in 1714 and wrote that it shows itself to the naked eye when the sky is clear and the moon away.
more: In a small telescope the edge of the ball crumbles into separate points. The center stays a solid glow. That is a real thing you are seeing, not a limit of the instrument. The stars near the middle really are crowded far closer together than the ones around here. To find it, look for the four stars of the Keystone in Hercules. M13 sits on the western side of that shape, about a third of the way down.

text: Charles Messier hunted comets, and he kept getting fooled by fuzzy patches that turned out to sit still. So he wrote a list of them, the things not to waste a night on. That annoyed list is now the most used catalogue in amateur astronomy: 110 objects, M1 to M110, every one worth looking at.
more: M1 is the Crab Nebula. M13 is the Hercules cluster. M31 is Andromeda. M42 is the Orion Nebula. M45 is the Pleiades. Messier built the bulk of the list between 1758 and 1782 and reached 103 entries. Other people added the last seven afterward, from his notes.

text: In December 1995 Hubble was aimed at a scrap of sky chosen because it looked empty, a spot about the apparent width of a dime seen from 75 feet. It stared at that nothing for ten days and took 342 exposures. The empty patch came back with roughly 3,000 galaxies in it.
more: The patch covers about one twenty-four-millionth of the whole sky. Spending ten days of a very expensive telescope on a blank spot was a genuine gamble. The director of the institute had to spend his own discretionary observing time to make it happen.

text: Some of the shapes in the sky are holes. The Coalsack, beside the Southern Cross, is a place where the Milky Way simply stops: a cloud of dust in the way, blocking everything behind it. Aboriginal Australians mapped it as the head of an emu whose body stretches on toward Scorpius.
more: Western constellations are made of bright stars. That tradition is made of the dark gaps between them, which needs a properly dark sky to see at all. The Coalsack is one of the few dark nebulae obvious to the unaided eye, and it is about 600 light-years off.

text: Go far enough south and you can see two fuzzy patches in the night sky. They look like torn-off pieces of the Milky Way lying on their own in the dark. You do not need a telescope. They are called the Magellanic Clouds.
more: Sailors on Magellan's ships wrote them down in 1519, which is where the name comes from. People living under southern skies had been watching them long before that. The bigger of the two is where the exploding star of 1987 appeared.

text: Nebula is just Latin for cloud, and for a long time it meant any fuzzy thing in a telescope. Then better instruments took the list apart. Some nebulae turned out to be swarms of stars too close together to separate. Others really are clouds of gas. They had been filed together for looking alike.
more: Lord Rosse had a 72-inch telescope in Ireland. In 1845 it showed a spiral shape inside M51. Nobody had seen that structure in one of these patches before. Until then the Pleiades, the Andromeda galaxy and the Orion Nebula all sat on the same fuzzy-patch lists. Nobody could tell them apart.

text: Photographs of nebulae are full of color. Through a telescope they are gray. Your eye has two kinds of light sensor, and the one that works in the dark cannot see color at all. A camera can sit collecting light for an hour; your eye starts over roughly every tenth of a second.
more: The Orion Nebula is bright enough to push a hint of green through to some people. Observers have argued for a long time about who can actually see it. Either way it is not a fault in the telescope. It is how eyes are built.

text: Right in the middle of the Orion Nebula, a small telescope shows four points of light in a tight lopsided box. They are called the Trapezium. A bigger telescope pulls two fainter ones out of the same small space. In binoculars all four blur into a single fuzzy dot.
more: The cloud is brightest close to those stars and dimmer further out. That is why their light is taken to be the cause. Nobody has watched the lighting happen. What has been measured is that the brightness falls off with distance exactly as it should if the stars are the source. Any telescope at all splits the fuzzy spot into four sharp stars in a wisp of gray cloud.

text: Job 38:31 asks, "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion?" Both are still up there and both still carry those names. You can go outside on a winter night and look at the two things the question is about. Very few old books can be checked that way.
more: Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8 name the same pair. Whoever wrote them was not describing something abstract. The Pleiades is a small knot of stars in Taurus. Orion is the brightest, most obvious figure in the winter sky. Neither one has moved.

text: Galileo's telescope was worse than a decent pair of binoculars. It magnified about twenty times and showed a keyhole of sky at a time. With that he found four points of light beside Jupiter that swapped places night after night, mountains on the moon, and Venus running through phases.
more: He published in March 1610, only weeks after the observations, which was unusually fast for the time. The four moons he called the Medicean Stars, after his patrons. Everybody else called them the Galilean moons, and that is the name that survived.
tryit: Brace a pair of binoculars against a fence or door frame and look at Jupiter. Three or four tiny dots strung out in a line beside it are the same moons Galileo saw. Look again the next night and they will have shuffled.

text: William Herschel was a working musician who ground his own mirrors. On 13 March 1781 he was sweeping through the sky from his garden in Bath. He found a small disk that was not a star. He reported it as a comet. It turned out to be a planet, the first ever found with a telescope.
more: Herschel wanted to call it Georgium Sidus after King George III. Other astronomers preferred Uranus, and Uranus won. The instrument was a reflector with a 6.2-inch mirror in a tube about seven feet long, made at home by hand.

text: The 200-inch Hale telescope on Palomar Mountain opened in 1948. It stayed the most capable telescope on Earth for 45 years. Its mirror is a single disk of Pyrex, over 16 feet across and weighing 14.5 tons. A honeycomb pattern is cast into the back to take weight out of it.
more: It is still working. Casting that disc at Corning took years and the first attempt failed outright. Every larger telescope built since has gone a different way: either a much thinner mirror held in shape by motors, or a mosaic of smaller ones.

text: The two Keck telescopes in Hawaii each carry a 33-foot (10 m) mirror that is not one mirror. It is 36 hexagons, held in line by motors that adjust them twice a second. A second, flexible mirror further down the light path bends hundreds of times a second to undo the blurring of the air.
more: To measure that blurring they fire a laser into the sky, lighting up sodium atoms about 56 miles up to make an artificial star exactly where they want one. The computer watches how the fake star wobbles and bends the flexible mirror to cancel the wobble out. Done well, the result beats Hubble for sharpness.

text: Hubble went up on 24 April 1990 with a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror ground to the wrong shape. Its edge was too flat by about four microns, a fiftieth the thickness of a hair, and every picture came back soft. In December 1993 astronauts flew up and fitted corrective optics to it.
more: The fix was called COSTAR, a set of small curved mirrors. They put exactly the opposite error into the light before it reached the instruments, like spectacles. It worked first time. Later instruments had the correction built into them. COSTAR was eventually taken out and put in a museum.

text: Webb's mirror is 21 feet 4 inches (6.5 m) across and it folds. It is 18 hexagons of beryllium under a skin of gold, each steered by seven motors. It sits about a million miles from Earth behind a five-layer sunshield the size of a tennis court, and it looks in infrared.
more: Infrared is heat, so the telescope has to be colder than anything it wants to look at. The sunshield holds a difference of roughly 570 degrees F between its hot side and its cold side. Nobody can fly out and fix it, so every one of the hundreds of unfolding steps after launch had to work first time. They did.

text: Some telescopes have no lens and no eyepiece, because they catch radio waves instead of light. The Green Bank dish in West Virginia is 328 feet (100 m) across, covers over two acres, and steers to any part of the sky. What comes out is a measurement, not a picture.
more: The 1,000-foot Arecibo dish in Puerto Rico was the largest single dish for over fifty years. Then its support cables gave way. The platform crashed into it on 1 December 2020. China's FAST is now the biggest, at 1,640 feet. It can only aim about 1,000 feet (300 m) of itself at a time.

text: Voyager 1 launched on 5 September 1977 and has never stopped. On 14 February 1990, from 3.7 billion miles out, it turned its camera around and photographed Earth. In the picture our planet is a speck less than one pixel across, sitting in a band of scattered sunlight.
more: Carl Sagan pushed for years to have that picture taken. There was no scientific reason for it and NASA repeatedly said no. The cameras were switched off permanently 34 minutes later to save power, and Voyager 1 is now the most distant object people have ever built.

text: John Bortle published a nine-step scale in Sky & Telescope in February 2001 to grade how dark a site is. Class 1 is the darkest ground left on Earth, where the Milky Way can cast a shadow. Class 9 is an inner city: the moon, the planets and a handful of stars.
more: Most suburbs land around class 5 or 6, where the Milky Way is a vague smear near the horizon or gone altogether. The difference between a class 5 sky and a class 3 sky is usually a forty-minute drive, and it is the single biggest upgrade available to any observer. To place your own sky: can you see the Milky Way at all, and can you find Andromeda without a chart? Count the stars inside the Great Square of Pegasus. Under a genuinely dark sky there are more than a dozen; from a city, none.

text: Your eyes take half an hour to switch over to night mode, and one glance at a phone undoes it. The sensors that work in the dark rely on a pigment that takes time to rebuild, and bright light bleaches it out in a second. Red light barely touches it, so observers use red flashlights.
tryit: Go outside, sit down, and do not look at any light at all for thirty minutes. Then look up. The same sky you glanced at on the way out will hold three or four times as many stars. You will not have changed anything but your own eyes.

text: The best first instrument is not a telescope. A pair of 10x50 binoculars costs a fraction as much and needs no setting up. It gives both eyes the same view. Brace your elbows on something and it stays steady enough. Nearly everything worth seeing in a night sky is within their reach.
more: The two numbers mean ten times magnification and 50-millimeter (2-inch) front lenses. The second number matters more, because it is how much light gets in. Anything above about 10x is hard to hold still, which is why 7x50 and 10x50 are the two sizes astronomers keep recommending.

text: A telescope's real job is collecting light, not magnifying. A 6-inch mirror gathers around 500 times as much light as a fully dark-adapted pupil. That is why it shows things the eye cannot reach at all. Magnification is a separate setting entirely. You change it by swapping the eyepiece.
more: Advertised magnifications like 525x on cheap telescopes are close to meaningless. Push a small instrument too far and you get a big, dim, mushy blob. The useful ceiling is roughly 50x per inch of aperture. Unsteady air normally stops you well below that anyway.

text: Big telescopes end up in awkward places for one reason: they need still, dry, dark air above them. Mauna Kea in Hawaii sits at 13,800 feet, high enough to make people ill. The Atacama in Chile is one of the driest deserts on Earth. Both are miserable to work at. Both give sharper pictures.
more: Water vapor in the air soaks up infrared. So a dry site sees colors a wet one cannot. Height gets you above part of the atmosphere and above most of the turbulence. Nobody builds a major observatory somewhere convenient. Convenient places have weather, water and streetlights.

text: Genesis 1:14 puts the lights in the sky "for signs and for seasons, and for days and years". Think of Galileo's little tube, the 200-inch Hale telescope, and Webb's folded gold mirror. Every instrument ever built for the sky is an extension of one plain activity. Going outside and looking up carefully.
more: The oldest working instrument is still the naked eye. It is not retired. Bessel's parallax, Goodricke's timing of Algol and the Chinese record of the guest star of 1054 all came from watching. So did every constellation ever named. Nothing but eyes, patience and somewhere to write it down.
